title: Why central banks are rediscovering the value of quiet money
body:
After a decade of aggressive intervention, central banks are quietly stepping back. Officials in Frankfurt, Washington and Tokyo now speak less often, move more deliberately and prefer to let markets do the talking. The shift is more than stylistic.

Behind the silence lies an unresolved intellectual problem. Inflation fell faster than most models predicted. Output held up while unemployment stayed low. The familiar Phillips curve, which traces the trade-off between prices and jobs, has flattened in almost every advanced economy since 2022.

That flattening has eroded confidence in two pillars of policy. First, the idea that interest rates can be tuned like a dial to cool or warm demand. Second, the assumption that central bankers can communicate their intentions clearly enough to shape expectations. When language itself becomes unreliable, less of it begins to look like a virtue.

Some hawks welcome the retreat. They argue that the credibility built up after the inflation of the 1970s and 1980s gives central banks the luxury of saying little. Doves disagree. They worry that an absence of guidance leaves households and businesses to construct their own narratives, often the wrong ones. A mortgage borrower who fears that rates will rise again may behave as if they will, even when the central bank intends otherwise.

Yet the quiet approach is not exactly new. In the late 1990s, when Alan Greenspan cultivated deliberate opacity, markets became unusually sensitive to tiny shifts in vocabulary. Words like "measured" or "imminent" moved bond yields more than entire policy statements do today. The lesson was that clarity, once lost, is hard to restore.

For now, central bankers seem prepared to live with the ambiguity. The cost of saying too much, they fear, is that they say the wrong thing. The cost of saying too little may turn out to be higher still, but it is harder to measure — which, in the world of modern central banking, may be why it is so tempting.

title: The small walking habit that changed how my family eats
body:
It started with a single block. After dinner, my wife suggested that we walk around the block together, just for ten minutes. The kids rolled their eyes. I shrugged and grabbed my shoes. The first night, we barely spoke. The second night, the kids came without being asked.

By the end of the first week, something had changed at the table. Conversation during dinner became easier. Arguments became shorter. We started talking about things that did not involve screens. None of this was planned.

I began reading about what researchers call a "transition ritual" — a small, repeatable action that signals the brain that one part of the day is over and another is beginning. A short walk turned out to be exactly that.

A month later, we had stopped ordering takeout on weeknights. Not because we decided to. We simply had time, and appetite, to cook. I had assumed the problem with our family dinners was the food. It turned out the problem was the gap between work and dinner, a gap we had been filling with phones.

Now, six months in, the habit has survived two holidays, a move, and a particularly persistent puppy. The walk is rarely longer than fifteen minutes. But I have come to think of it as the most important part of our day.

If you are trying to change a family routine, my advice is this: do not start with a big plan. Start with a small walk. The rest of the evening will follow.

title: Beijing expands urban green corridors to ease summer heat
body:
Beijing has unveiled a three-year plan to expand its network of urban green corridors, adding more than 400 kilometers of shaded walkways that connect parks, rivers and residential neighborhoods. Officials say the project is designed to make the capital more livable during increasingly hot summers.

The plan focuses on narrow strips of land along old city walls, railway lines and canals. Many of these spaces have been neglected for decades. Under the new scheme, they will be replanted with native trees and equipped with water features, benches and cycle paths.

City planners say the corridors will serve two purposes. They will provide pedestrians with shaded routes to nearby parks, reducing the need for cars. They will also create wind channels that help cool surrounding blocks, a low-cost alternative to mechanical air conditioning.

The project builds on similar initiatives in other Chinese cities, including Shanghai and Chengdu. Studies from those cities suggest that even a modest increase in tree cover can lower surface temperatures by several degrees during the afternoon peak.

For residents, the most visible change will be in older neighborhoods, where narrow streets often trap heat. "We have always known that our hutong felt hotter than the wider roads," said one longtime resident. "Now there will be trees, and water, and somewhere for the children to walk after dinner."

Construction is expected to begin next spring, with the first sections opening to the public by the end of next year.
